title: Privacy and Copyright Protection in Generative AI: A Lifecycle Perspective
venue: 2024 IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering - Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing privacy and copyright risks created by generative AI systems that are trained on large-scale datasets collected from the web. The authors argue that existing protections such as differential privacy, machine unlearning, and data poisoning are fragmented and typically address only isolated points in the AI development process.

Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention or an educational technology study, the paper proposes a lifecycle perspective for understanding and mitigating these risks. It maps privacy and copyright challenges onto stages of the data lifecycle, including problem formulation, data collection, cleaning, annotation, model training, evaluation, deployment/inference, and distribution. The paper discusses issues such as consent and license acquisition, transparency and access, consent withdrawal, provenance and attribution, side effects of protection methods, continuous monitoring, and downstream distribution.

The paper’s context is generative AI more broadly, especially large language models and other foundation models, with examples drawn from legal and technical discussions in the EU GDPR and US copyright law. It concludes that robust privacy and copyright protection will require integrated, lifecycle-aware approaches, including consent management, machine forgetting, guardrails, and AI bills of materials. No human participants, educational population, or school setting are studied.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a peer-reviewed conference position/framework article, but it does not report a formal empirical study, comparison, or measured outcomes. Its claims are argumentative and synthesis-based rather than based on a testable evaluation design.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational impact is measured, and the paper does not evaluate any intervention on student, teacher, or institutional outcomes. Its contribution is primarily conceptual guidance for AI governance, not demonstrated impact.

interventions.use_case: A lifecycle framework for privacy and copyright protection in generative AI, focusing on consent acquisition, transparency, machine unlearning, provenance/attribution, guardrails, monitoring, and AI bill of materials across model development and deployment.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual / position paper rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not report measured effects on learners or institutions. It argues that current privacy and copyright protections in GenAI are fragmented and that lifecycle-integrated governance mechanisms are needed, but provides no sample sizes, effect sizes, or outcome data.
